titre: Thirty years after the moratorium, the cod have not come back
accroche: In 1992, Newfoundland closes its cod fishery. The stock was believed capable of rebounding as soon as it was left alone
contenu_vulgarise:
The Grand Banks of Newfoundland fed Europe for five centuries. Cod had been fished there since the 1500s, and the stock seemed inexhaustible.

Catches peaked at more than 800,000 metric tons in 1968, driven by factory trawlers able to work the open sea in all weather. Then they declined.

On July 2, 1992, Canada's fisheries minister announced a moratorium. It was supposed to last two years.

## What the numbers were already saying

Spawning biomass had dropped by about 93% in three decades.

What makes the case exemplary is not ignorance. It is what was done with what was known. Fisheries biologists produced annual advice. The quotas set were regularly higher than what they recommended, under understandable social and political pressure: thirty thousand direct jobs in a province of half a million people.

A methodological weakness was added to this. Estimates relied in part on catches reported by fishers, set against fishing effort. But as techniques improved, fish kept being found where they remained concentrated, which gave the illusion of stable abundance while the overall stock collapsed.

## What didn't happen next

The moratorium's implicit assumption was simple: remove the pressure, and the population rebounds.

It did not rebound, or only very slowly. The moratorium, planned for two years, lasted thirty-two years.

Several explanations combine, and none suffices alone. A very small population reproduces poorly, for reasons that have to do with finding mates and with age structure. Fishing took the large individuals first, the most fecund, so that the surviving stock was made up of young, unproductive fish. And the ecosystem had reorganized: shrimp and crabs, which cod fed on, thrived, and in turn eat juvenile cod.

This last point is the most disturbing. The system did not simply slide down a slope that it could climb back up. It shifted into another state, one that sustains itself.

## What the case changed

Fisheries management drew a costly lesson from it: a stock is not a tap you can turn back on.

Hence the so-called precautionary approach, now written into law: setting thresholds before they are needed, taking uncertainty into account rather than adopting the most favorable estimate, and ceasing to treat an ecosystem as a stock of goods independent of one another.

repere.texte: Catches peak at more than 800,000 metric tons in 1968. The spawning biomass of northern cod drops by about 93% in thirty years. The moratorium, announced for two years in 1992, lasted thirty-two years.
repere.source: Encyclopædia Britannica, “Cod fishery collapse of 1992”; Newfoundland and Labrador Heritage, “Cod Moratorium”

carte.punch: Fishing stopped in 1992. Thirty years later, the cod had not come back.
carte.idee: The Grand Banks stock collapsed by 93% in thirty years, on quotas set above scientific advice. Removing fishing was not enough: the ecosystem had shifted into another state, one that sustains itself.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Heritage Newfoundland and Labrador — Cod Moratorium
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: In English; the moratorium's effect on fishing communities, seen from the province.

quiz.question: Why didn't the stock rebound after fishing stopped?
choix: Because illegal fishing continued despite the moratorium
Because warming waters moved the cod northward
Because the moratorium was enforced on only part of the Grand Banks
Because the ecosystem had reorganized into a state that sustains itself
quiz.explication: Shrimp and crabs, which cod fed on, thrived and in turn eat its juveniles. On top of that, the age structure was depleted: fishing had taken the large individuals, the most fecund. Removing the pressure does not return the system to its earlier state, which is what makes the case so costly.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what year did Grand Banks cod catches reach their maximum?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Catches peak at more than 800,000 metric tons in 1968, before a decline that would lead to the 1992 moratorium, twenty-four years later.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did fishing quotas set before 1992 regularly exceed the biologists' advice?
choix: Because the biologists systematically overestimated the state of the stock
Because scientific data was passed on only once a decade
Under social pressure from a province where fishing supports thirty thousand direct jobs
Because no law required the government to consult biologists
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The quotas set regularly exceeded the recommendations of fisheries biologists, under understandable social and political pressure in a fishing province.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What methodological bias gave the illusion of a stable stock while it was collapsing?
choix: Fishers deliberately underreported their catches to the authorities
As techniques improved, fish were still found where they remained concentrated
Scientific surveys were carried out in only one area of the Grand Banks
Underwater measuring instruments gave erratic results in bad weather
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Estimates relied on catches set against fishing effort, but improved techniques made it possible to find concentrated fish, masking the overall collapse.
